--- title: "Inspect the model" subtitle: "Read response shapes, design structure, contrast weights, and sampling times." jupyter: python3 execute: freeze: auto --- Plot the model before interpreting its statistics: check the response shape, event timing, column structure, correlations, and contrast weights. These helpers return Matplotlib figures. For the fitted-model plots, see the [figure gallery](plot-gallery.qmd). On narrow screens, scroll plots horizontally to read their labels. Select a plot for the complete view. ## Follow events into regressors ::: {#5ac84ee3 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import pandas as pd import fmrimod as fm from fmrimod.hrf import get_hrf from fmrimod.plotting import plot_hrf, plot_hrfs from fmrimod.spec import compile as compile_spec from fmrimod.spec import hrf from fmrimod.visualization import ( correlation_map, design_correlations, design_map, plot_event_model, plot_sampling_frame, ) events = pd.DataFrame({ "onset": [0.0, 10.0, 20.0, 30.0], "condition": ["face", "scene", "face", "scene"], "duration": 2.0, }) sampling = fm.SamplingFrame(blocklens=60, TR=1.0) event_model, _ = compile_spec(hrf("condition", basis="spmg1"), data=events, sampling_frame=sampling) ``` ::: ::: {#d009ef39 .cell fig-height='3.2' fig-width='7' execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig = plot_event_model(event_model, figsize=(7, 3.2)) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Realized face and scene regressors on the acquisition grid, one row per condition. Ticks under each row mark that condition's onsets and bars their 2 s durations, so each response can be traced to its event.](plotting-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){fig-alt='Two stacked line charts, face above scene, each showing two hemodynamic responses over sixty seconds with onset ticks underneath.'} ::: ::: `style="overlay"` puts every regressor on one amplitude axis instead, and `style="heatmap"` (chosen automatically for large designs such as trialwise models) draws one raster row per regressor. ## View the design as a matrix `design_map()` draws the matrix itself, one row per scan and one column per regressor, the way SPM shows it. Each column is divided by its largest absolute value so columns in different units share one colour scale; the grey bars underneath keep the real magnitudes visible, and a column that is nearly flat next to the rest of its term is marked in orange. ::: {#6a37ea73 .cell fig-height='6.6' fig-width='5.4' execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig = design_map(event_model) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The face and scene columns of the design matrix, scans running downward. Bars under the matrix compare each column's peak with the largest in its term.](plotting-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){fig-alt='Heatmap with two columns, face and scene, showing alternating red bands where each condition\'s responses occur, with a colour bar below.'} ::: ::: The same call works on a `BaselineModel`, where drift and intercept columns are grouped by run, and on a full `FmriModel`. ## Inspect column correlations `correlation_map()` shows every pair of regressors once, as the lower triangle of the correlation matrix. Pairs at or above `|r| = 0.5` are outlined, and the diagonal carries each column's variance inflation factor (VIF), which catches collinearity that no single pair reveals; VIFs of 5 or more turn orange. ::: {#c8210b4e .cell fig-height='3.6' fig-width='5.4' execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig = correlation_map(event_model) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Pairwise correlation and diagonal VIF values for the alternating face and scene regressors. Inspect these alongside numerical rank; pairwise correlations alone do not establish estimability.](plotting-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){fig-alt='A single shaded cell giving the face-scene correlation, with the variance inflation factor of each regressor on the diagonal.'} ::: ::: The numbers are available without a plot: ::: {#bd5a9707 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} design_correlations(event_model).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
face scene
face 1.00 -0.43
scene -0.43 1.00
``` ::: ::: ## Check contrast weights `plot_contrasts()` lays each contrast out as a row of weights over the same columns. Two margin columns check every row: `sum w` (a non-zero sum, in orange, means the contrast is not a pure comparison) and `SE ×σ`, the standard error the design gives the contrast per unit of noise; lower is better. An `EventModel` with contrasts on its terms can be passed directly; here the weights are given by hand, with the model supplying the design. ::: {#a0362985 .cell fig-height='2.6' fig-width='6.5' execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} from fmrimod.contrast import plot_contrasts fig = plot_contrasts( {"face_vs_scene": [1, -1], "face": [1, 0]}, labels=["face", "scene"], design=event_model, ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![A face-versus-scene comparison and the face effect alone. The comparison sums to zero; the single-condition contrast does not.](plotting-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-8-output-1.png){fig-alt='Two rows of contrast weights over the face and scene columns, with sum and standard-error columns at the right.'} ::: ::: ## Check the acquisition grid The sampling-frame plot is useful when a model has multiple runs or unusual TRs. It reads the timing object already used by design construction. Here three runs, one of them shorter: the odd run is set in bold and the caption says why, and passing the event table draws each onset under its run, so a run without events or with an empty tail stands out. ::: {#fc4dc041 .cell fig-height='2.9' fig-width='7.6' execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} runs = fm.SamplingFrame(blocklens=[60, 60, 40], TR=1.0) run_events = pd.DataFrame({ "onset": [5.0, 20.0, 40.0, 8.0, 30.0, 50.0, 12.0], "run": [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3], }) fig = plot_sampling_frame(runs, events=run_events) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Three runs on one time axis. The third run is 20 scans short (bold), and the ticks under each bar show where the events fall.](plotting-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.png){fig-alt='Three horizontal bars, one per run, laid end to end on a time axis, with small onset ticks beneath each bar.'} ::: ::: `style="grid"` shows each run's scans as cells on a within-run axis instead, and `style="lane"` packs the runs into one annotated row. ## Inspect baseline terms The baseline model holds the drift, intercept and nuisance columns. Its plot draws every time-varying term on the shared time axis, one panel per term, and lists the constant terms (here the run intercepts) in the caption, together with the high-pass period the drift basis roughly corresponds to. ::: {#ef0f7eed .cell fig-height='4' fig-width='7.6' execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} baseline = fm.baseline_model(basis="poly", degree=3, sframe=runs) fig = baseline.plot() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Cubic polynomial drift, three columns per run. Each run gets its own copy, and no line crosses a run boundary.](plotting-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.png){fig-alt='Line chart of three polynomial drift curves repeated in each of three runs, with a key at the right edge.'} ::: ::: `design_map(baseline)` and `correlation_map(baseline)` show the same columns as a matrix and as within-run correlations. ## Inspect the HRF basis The `fmrimod.plotting` module covers HRF and regressor plots. Use it to inspect an HRF object before it is convolved into a design. Each function returns a matplotlib `Figure`. ::: {#42c29e93 .cell fig-height='3.8' fig-width='6' execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig = plot_hrf(get_hrf("spmg1"), normalize=True) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Normalized SPM canonical HRF: a positive peak followed by a smaller undershoot. This is the response shape used by the design above.](plotting-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-11-output-1.png){fig-alt='Line chart of the normalized SPM canonical hemodynamic response, rising to one positive peak near five seconds, annotated with the peak time, and falling through a shallow undershoot.'} ::: ::: A basis set expands to one curve per basis function, labelled at its peak, so you can see what each column of a multi-basis term models. ::: {#ed0debf8 .cell fig-height='4.2' fig-width='7' execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig = plot_hrfs(get_hrf("spmg3")) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The SPMG3 basis: the canonical response with its temporal and dispersion derivatives, which absorb small shifts in latency and width.](plotting-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-12-output-1.png){fig-alt='Three curves labelled canonical, temporal deriv. and dispersion deriv.; the derivatives oscillate around zero within the canonical response\'s time window.'} ::: ::: ## Inspect fitted estimates - [Figure gallery](plot-gallery.qmd): model plots, coefficient distributions, fitted HRFs, observed and fitted signals, and residual autocorrelation. - [Rank and residuals](linear-model.qmd#inspect-rank-and-conditioning). - [Contrast explanations](contrasts.qmd#read-the-contrast-explanation). - [Smooth FIR response estimates](estimating-hrfs.qmd). - [Trial amplitudes](single-trial.qmd#plot-trial-estimates). - [Subject surprise and influence](group-diagnostics.qmd). ## Next - [Design matrices](design-matrices.qmd) - [Overview and workflow](overview-workflow.qmd)
